hints: Look at Fig. 3.1 and count how many intermediate forms exist between winged and wingless - are plants either one type or the other, or is there a smooth range in between?
walkthrough:
Spot Distinct Categories With No Intermediates**
You are sitting with two clear phenotypes side by side, winged fruit or wingless fruit. There is no in-between fruit, no half-winged type. That pattern is controlled by a single gene with two alleles, so the phenotype falls into separate groups.

Link To Variation Type**
When a characteristic shows distinct, non-overlapping phenotypes with no intermediates and is controlled by one or few genes, we call it discontinuous variation. That is different from continuous variation like height, which shows a full range and is polygenic plus environmental.

hints: Start by thinking where completely new genetic information comes from in a population if no humans are involved.
Next think how existing alleles for colour in different plants could be brought together naturally to make a new combination in offspring.
walkthrough:
Create A Brand New Allele By Mutation**
DNA copying is very accurate but random changes in base sequence can happen during replication. A mutation in a gene controlling pigment production can create a new allele, which can give a new fruit colour when expressed.

Mix Existing Alleles By Crossing**
Sea blush is a flowering plant, so pollen can be transferred between different plants by wind or insects. This cross-pollination, including hybridisation between slightly different populations, brings different colour alleles together in one zygote. Random fertilisation and meiosis then produce new allele combinations, for example bringing two codominant alleles together to give a new phenotype.
Final answer: mutation forming a new allele for fruit colour; cross-pollination / hybridisation leading to new allele combinations in offspring.

hints: Recall the biological definition of a species - what test of breeding would prove two different-looking plants are really the same species?
Think beyond fruit shape - what other features of whole plants living in the same place would you compare?
Think about the most powerful modern evidence inside cells that shows two organisms share the same genome.
walkthrough:
Use The Breeding Test For Species**
The biological species concept says members of the same species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring. If winged-fruit plants and wingless-fruit plants cross and the offspring are fertile, they are not reproductively isolated, so the fruit difference is just polymorphism within one species.

Compare Ecology And Body Plan**
Members of one species share a way of life and basic structure. Finding that both types occupy the same niche on the west coast and share the same morphology, physiology and biochemistry apart from the single fruit-wing gene supports one species. Early taxonomists were misled by focusing only on fruit shape.

Compare Molecules**
The strongest confirmation comes from molecules. If DNA base sequences, whole genomes, and the resulting amino acid sequences of proteins are the same or very similar between the two types, that shows they share a recent common gene pool and belong to the same species.

Final answer: any three from: can interbreed to produce fertile offspring and are not reproductively isolated; occupy the same niche; have same / similar morphology, physiology or biochemistry; have similar / same genes, DNA sequences or genomes; have similar / same proteins or amino acid sequences.

hints: Start with numbers - what happens when plants produce far more seeds and offspring than can possibly survive?
Think about why those offspring are not all identical and where those differences come from.
Link large numbers plus limited resources to what individuals must do to stay alive.
Consider why some individuals cope with that struggle better than others in a particular environment.
Finish by thinking what happens to the alleles of the survivors in the next generation.
walkthrough:
Overproduction Creates The Struggle**
Plants like sea blush can produce very many seeds and offspring. Resources such as light, water, minerals, space and pollinators are limited, so there is competition and an environmental selection pressure.

Variation Provides The Raw Material**
Offspring are not genetically identical. Variation arises from random mutations and from sexual reproduction - crossing over, independent assortment in meiosis and random fertilisation. So some plants inherit slightly different phenotypes, for example in fruit, growth or resistance.

Differential Survival And Reproduction**
In that particular environment, some phenotypes are better adapted. Individuals with an advantageous adaptation have a selective advantage, so they are more likely to survive to flowering and produce more seeds than less well adapted individuals. This is natural selection.

Inheritance Changes Allele Frequencies**
Survivors pass their advantageous alleles to offspring through gametes. Because they contribute more offspring, the frequency of the advantageous allele in the population gene pool increases over generations, while disadvantageous alleles decrease.

Build The Full Causal Chain**
Put together for full marks: many offspring -> genetic variation -> competition plus selection pressure -> advantageous phenotype survives and reproduces -> advantageous alleles inherited and increase in frequency. That directional change is why natural selection occurs.

Final answer: populations produce many offspring; genetic variation exists due to mutation, meiosis and random fertilisation; competition for resources and selection pressure occurs; individuals with advantageous phenotypes survive and reproduce; they pass on advantageous alleles so allele frequency increases.
